hero_title: Use the AI on the real work.
hero_lede: A swarm of agents doesn't jam because the agents aren't smart enough. It jams at the same few deterministic points: who has the file, whose copy is stale, what merges, which tests to run. codeSplitter takes those points over with plain code, so they unclog, and your AI spends its tokens on the feature. It still hooks in wherever you want a judgement call.
scene_unclog_title: Unclog the file, not the work
scene_unclog_text: The old way, two agents each take the whole file and fight over it on the way back. Here every line is its own record, so each one lands its own lines and nobody waits. codeSplitter only does the logistics: the AI still writes every line.
scene_drift_title: Branch at lightning speed. Then the noise.
scene_drift_text: Artifacts makes a branch a real git repo in milliseconds. Left alone, the copies drift out of tune: their waves cancel, the signal shrinks, and the light dims as the work leaks out of the line. Your AI gets pulled off features, security and maintenance into the plumbing: merge fights and rewriting what someone just rewrote. We all clog it. Watch the scope.
scene_lock_title: Coordinate, and the signal comes back
scene_lock_text: Durable Objects keep one live copy of each file and Mervin settles the merges, so the harmonics line up and boost each other. The light gets bright, every electron gets through, and the AI checks in, finds nothing the matter, and goes back to features, security and maintenance. You still plug the AI in, just not nearly as often.
scene_mervin_text: Not a model: plain rules, as fast as the computer goes. Changes that don't clash go together in one wave; the ones that do wait a wave; the rare real clash comes back as one card.
scene_hook_title: Hook your AI in, or don't
scene_hook_text: After Mervin, before Ester, after Ester: three places a hook can say yay or nay. Off, an AI's call, or a person's. Use the AI where it's judgement, not traffic.
scene_ester_title: Ester stacks the tests in lanes
scene_ester_text: Some tests run on every change. Some every fifth, because they add up. Some only at a release: the iOS app two days before the preview. And the bus takes no tests at all: changes ride along until it's full, then one big AI pass over all of them.
scene_yours_text: One more hook if you want it, then ship, deploy, release. Every stop on the way was a plain call: CLI, API, MCP or code mode, the same answer each time.
road_blurb: Every change, an agent's or a person's, goes down the same road. Each stop is deterministic: same inputs, same answer, no model, no tokens. The dashed ones are where your AI can say yay or nay.
stop_branch_text:
A branch is a real git repo, made in milliseconds. A thousand agents can each have one.

On its own, every copy starts drifting from the others the moment it's made.
stop_coordinate_text:
Each file's lines live in one place, on a tiny computer every agent talks to. Edits land in order, line by line, so nobody fights over a file and nobody waits on someone else's copy.

Watch the dots
stop_mervin_text:
Merges by line id. Changes that don't clash go together in one wave, the ones that do wait a wave, and the rare real clash comes back as a card.

His case file
stop_hook1_text: Review the merged change, or have the last word before the tests spend anything. Off, ai or ask.
stop_ester_text:
Runs only the lanes this change calls for, and sorts any red by whose it is: main's, flaky, the PR's own, or the merge's.

Her case file
stop_hook2_text: It's green. Does an AI or a person still want to look before it ships?
stop_yours_text: Ship it, deploy it, release it. From here on it's yours, however you like to work.
lanes_title: Test lanes: not every test, every time
lanes_blurb: Running every test on every change is how a swarm waits on its slowest suite. Ester gives each set of tests a cadence instead.
lane_always_runs: every change that touches its paths
lane_always_for: the tests you never want to go without
lane_often_runs: every Nth change, and at every release; the skipped ones are owed
lane_often_for: the slow ones that add up: stress runs, the end-to-end journey
lane_release_runs: only when a release is cut
lane_release_for: what you don't care about until then: the iOS app, two days before the preview
lane_bus_runs: no tests per change. Changes take a seat, and when it's full (or a release is cut) the bus leaves: one big pass over all of them, an AI's if the lane has no command
lane_bus_for: docs, copy, the long tail nobody tests by hand
config_file: A repo keeps its road in codesplitter.pipeline.json at the top of main. Without one: no hooks, one lane that tests everything.
config_ask: Then ask what a change does, from wherever you work. The same plain answer each time.
config_answer: The answer lists every stop, the hooks that are on, and each lane's call (run, skip, board or depart), with the counts to send with the next change. The API reference · MCP
why_title: Why the AI goes around the stops
why_text: Whether two edits touch the same line, or whether a red check was already red on main, is a lookup, not a judgement. A model would spend tokens and minutes on it, and every agent behind it waits. So the lookups are code, and the hooks hand an AI or a person only what is truly a judgement call: is this change right, is it ready, should it ship. The git problems a swarm hits · a real week of 1,000 PRs
footer: Today the API answers the plan: which stops, which hooks are on, what each lane does (src/pipeline.ts). Running the hooks and lanes from it is next (#3313), and so is a merge train, so a newer PR's green still holds once an older one lands (#3314). The scene's changes are made up; its lane calls are that same code.
